Johnson tells Sen. Everett Dirksen that Hoover worries congressional investigations will reflect on him, and that there are international complications to be careful of.
Learning that Chief Justice Warren refuses to serve, Johnson summons him for 4:30.
The palm print lifted from the rifle reaches the FBI lab, three days after all other Dallas evidence.

A Hoover memo to the State Department says the FBI briefed "Mr. George Bush of the Central Intelligence Agency" on Miami exile reaction. The CIA later said this referred to a different George Bush, a junior employee.
An unnamed source cited in the chronology claims George H.W. Bush worked with the CIA from 1960–61 using his oil company as cover; this is not established.

Hoover records Johnson's summary: Oswald did it; Connally was hit after the President; Kennedy would have been hit three times had Connally not turned. Around now Robert Kennedy sends Bill Walton to Moscow to tell Soviet contact Georgi Bolshakov that he and Mrs. Kennedy believe a large conspiracy killed the President (per Talbot, Brothers).

Jack Martin, apparently frightened, tells the Secret Service his Ferrie story came from drunken "telephonitis." A Dallas FBI teletype reports the .38 revolver found in a paper bag near the assassination area on November 23.
It is the same model as the revolver taken from Oswald; only the serial numbers differ.
Oswald's revolver bears serial number V510210.

Times Herald editor A.C. Greene says readers sent Mrs. Tippit over $200,000 and Marina Oswald about as much. C.L. Connell tells the FBI Silvia Odio knew Oswald, and mentions a suspicious "Mr. Martin" seeking guns for exiles; the FBI does not interview Odio until December 19.
The chronology notes that Watergate burglar James McCord used the alias Edward J. Martin and E. Howard Hunt was said to use "Mr. White," names an informant later linked to a 1972 provocation plan.
Hoover and Johnson discuss the proposed commission. Johnson calls Hoover more a brother than FBI chief. Once the commissioners are named, Hoover has dossiers compiled on each.

Hoover's memo of the call: Johnson wants to rely on the FBI report and stop congressional probes with a high-level panel; they discuss Dulles, McCloy, Norstad, Boggs, Ford, Russell and Cooper. Hoover says Mexico City leads, including Alvarado's $6,500 story and Sylvia Duran's re-arrest, are delaying the report.
Hoover dismisses polygraphs, calls Ruby a seedy egomaniac friendly with police, notes officers beside Oswald did nothing until the shot, and says the morning move was made for the cameras.

Hoover says three shots were fired, the first and third hitting Kennedy and the second Connally; that a whole bullet fell from the President's head onto the stretcher; that the shots were found on the fifth floor; and that the shots could be fired in three seconds. Several of these statements conflict with the later official account.
He recounts the arrest at the Texas Theatre and says Oswald took the stairs.
On a Cuban money link, Hoover says it is unproven; Marina will cooperate if assured she can stay in the U.S.
Hoover says a workman saw Oswald on the fifth floor, notes no agents rode the limousine's rear, and urges Johnson to use a bulletproof car.
Hoover recommends armored cars, including at the ranch, and guarded entrances; Johnson asks for his thoughts in writing.

Johnson presses Warren to chair the commission, citing rumors involving Khrushchev and Castro and McNamara's estimate that a nuclear first strike would kill 60 million Americans; Warren reportedly leaves in tears. John Newman and others argue that the threat of war became the pretext for accepting a lone-gunman account.
Johnson asks Allen Dulles to serve; he agrees.
Gerald Ford agrees to serve. Johnson releases the executive order, drafted by Abe Fortas, in time for Saturday's papers.
